items.title: Causative agent: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense
items.contentHtml:
Trypanosoma brucei gambiense

  • Trypanosoma brucei gambiense is the agent of the chronic or West African form of African trypanosomiasis; It has a slow evolution (years).
  • The subspecies Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense causes the acute or East African form, with rapid progression to disease of the central nervous system.
  • The parasite is an extracellular flagellated protozoan; evades the immune response through antigenic variation of the variant surface glycoprotein (VSG).
  • Trypanosoma brucei gambiense is the most common cause in humans; The main reservoir is human, unlike Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense which has an animal reservoir.

items.title: Vector transmission
items.contentHtml:
Transmission by tsetse fly

  • Transmission is by the bite of the tsetse fly of the genus Glossina; Both subspecies are transmitted by different vectors: Glossina palpalis for Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and Glossina morsitans for Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense.
  • The tsetse fly becomes infected by feeding on blood from an infected host; The parasite develops in the intestine of the vector and migrates to the salivary glands, where it becomes metacyclic.
  • Transmission can also be mechanical by other insects, congenital or by blood transfusions, although it is uncommon.
  • The geographical distribution is limited to sub-Saharan Africa, in rural areas with dense vegetation and humidity, the habitat of the vector.

items.foco: Hemolymphatic phase with fever and lymphadenopathy
items.title: hemolymphatic phase
items.contentHtml:
Hemolymphatic phase

  • The hemolymphatic phase (stage 1) occurs after the spread of the parasite through blood and lymph; It is characterized by intermittent fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, headache, arthralgia and pruritus.
  • The fever is irregular and may disappear spontaneously, which delays the diagnosis; parasites appear in peripheral blood in spikes.
  • Lymphadenopathy is more prominent in the gambian form, especially in the posterior cervical region.
  • Other findings include hepatosplenomegaly, annular erythema (trypanide), and facial edema; Anemia and thrombocytopenia are common.
  • The distinction with the meningoencephalic phase is made by examining the cerebrospinal fluid, not by clinical signs alone.

items.foco: Winterbottom sign in cervical lymph nodes
items.title: Winterbottom sign
items.contentHtml:
Winterbottom sign

  • The Winterbottom sign is the presence of painless and mobile posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, typical of Trypanosoma brucei gambiense infection.
  • The lymphadenopathy is located in the posterior cervical triangle; histologically it shows follicular hyperplasia with lymphocytes and plasma cells.
  • It is an early but not pathognomonic clinical finding; It can appear in other infections (tuberculosis, lymphoma).
  • Aspiration of the lymph node can demonstrate the parasite in the aspirate, useful for parasitological diagnosis.

items.title: meningoencephalic phase
items.contentHtml:
Meningoencephalic phase

  • The meningoencephalic phase (stage 2) occurs when the parasite invades the central nervous system; It is characterized by sleep disorders (inversion of the circadian rhythm: daytime sleepiness, nocturnal insomnia), hence the name “sleeping illness”.
  • Other neurological symptoms: severe headache, tremor, ataxia, extrapyramidal rigidity, seizures and psychiatric disorders (apathy, aggressiveness).
  • The diagnosis is confirmed by examination of the fluid. cerebrospinal (CSF): pleocytosis >5 cells/µL and presence of parasites or increased IgM.
  • Without treatment, the outcome is fatal; progressive encephalopathy leads to coma and death.

items.foco: Diagnosis by thick smear and blood smear
items.title: Parasitological diagnosis
items.contentHtml:
Diagnosis by thick smear and smear

  • The thick smear and blood smear are the gold standard for detecting the parasite in blood; Motile trypomastigotes are observed fresh or stained with Giemsa.
  • The thick smear is more sensitive than the thin smear because it concentrates more blood; It is recommended to examine at least 100 fields.
  • The parasite can be scarce and cyclical; Should repeated samples be taken (every 6 hours) or concentration methods used (microhematocrit, QBC).
  • Does the thick smear allow morphological differentiation between Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense? No; The differentiation is geographical and clinical, not morphological.

items.title: CATT test
items.contentHtml:
CATT rapid test

  • The cardaglutinin test for trypanosomiasis (CATT) is a rapid serological test in whole blood, serum or plasma, which detects antibodies against Trypanosoma brucei gambiense.
  • It is based on the agglutination of particles coated with variant surface antigens (LiTat 1.3); It is sensitive for the gambiense form, but not for Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense.
  • A positive result requires parasitological confirmation (thick smear, lymph node aspirate) because there may be false positives due to other infections or cross reactions.
  • The CATT rapid test is useful for screening in the field and in blood banks, but does not replace microscopic examination.

items.title: CSF Staging
items.contentHtml:
CSF cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
  • The IgM in CSF (increased) and the presence of antibodies are also evaluated; proteinorraquia may be elevated.
  • CSF should be processed immediately; Centrifugation increases sensitivity to detect parasites.
  • Staging is crucial because treatment differs: drugs that do not cross the blood-brain barrier are ineffective in stage 2.

items.foco: First stage treatment: pentamidine or suramin
items.title: Stage 1 treatment
items.contentHtml:
First stage treatment

  • In the hemolymphatic phase (stage 1), the treatment of choice is pentamidine for Trypanosoma brucei gambiense infection; It is administered intramuscularly at a dose of 4 mg/kg/day for 7 days.
  • For Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense, suramine is used at a dose of 20 mg/kg (test dose of 100-200 mg) intravenously, in a schedule of 5 doses every 3-7 days.
  • Pentamidine does not cross the blood-brain barrier well, so it is only useful in stage 1; can cause hypoglycemia and nephrotoxicity.
  • Suramin is contraindicated in Onchocerca volvulus infection (risk of severe reaction) and is associated with proteinuria.

items.title: Stage 2 treatment
items.contentHtml:
Second stage treatment

  • For meningoencephalic phase (stage 2) due to Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, the treatment of choice is eflornithine (difluoromethylornithine, DFMO) in combination with nifurtimox (nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy, NECT).
  • The regimen for eflornithine in monotherapy is 400 mg/kg/day intravenously in 4 doses for 14 days; the combination reduces duration and toxicity.
  • For Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense, the drug of choice is melarsoprol (trivalent arsenic) at a dose of 2.2 mg/kg/day intravenously for 10 days.
  • melarsoprol is highly toxic and is associated with reactive encephalopathy; eflornithine is not effective against Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense.

items.title: Melarsoprol toxicity
items.contentHtml:
Melarsoprol and reactive encephalopathy

  • Melarsoprol is an arsenical compound used in stage 2, especially for Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense; Its most serious adverse effect is reactive encephalopathy.
  • Reactive encephalopathy occurs in 5-10% of patients, with seizures, coma and high mortality (10-50%).
  • Its mechanism is attributed to an immune/inflammatory reaction due to the massive destruction of parasites in the central nervous system, not to direct toxicity.
  • Prevention includes administering corticosteroids. (prednisolone) concomitant and premedicate with antitrypanosomal agents; Close monitoring is recommended.
  • Melarsoprol is administered in a propylene glycol solution, by slow intravenous route.

items.foco: Prevention with vector control and screening
items.title: Prevention and control
items.contentHtml:
Prevention with vector control and screening

  • Prevention is based on vector control using tsetse fly traps, insecticides and habitat modification.
  • Active screening of populations at risk with serological tests (CATT) and parasitological diagnosis allows early cases to be detected and reduced transmission.
  • Personal protection includes repellents, long-sleeved clothing, and avoiding endemic areas; There is no vaccine.
  • The control of animal reservoirs is relevant for Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense; Health education is essential.
  • Epidemiological surveillance and early treatment of cases are pillars for eliminating the disease as a public health problem.
